prize_parts.citation: For showing, with transparent local-labour-market designs, how technological change and import competition reshape labour demand, job polarisation and the adjustment of workers and regions.

statement.case_for: B006 is still my preferred single part. My round-1 file ranked it first, and I have changed one name: Dorn replaces Katz. The reasons are scientific and about credit, not about how many colleagues prefer Katz. The achievement I can defend most precisely is a design-based account of how exposure to technology and trade shifts labour demand and where the adjustment costs fall. Autor and Hanson anchor the import-competition work. Dorn is a lead co-author of the China-shock papers. He also co-authored with Autor the work on the polarisation of the labour market and the growth of low-skill service jobs, so in my reading he spans the technology and trade strands that several colleagues worry may be two discoveries. That is my own reading of the credited names and I have not verified it independently. It is the strongest argument I can offer for treating the pair of lines as one body of work. Katz's separate claim is the long-run supply-and-demand account of the skill premium and the race between education and technology. That claim is real and mature, but his best-known education-technology work was done with a recent laureate (Goldin, 2023). A citation naming him therefore invites the question of what it adds beyond that prize. The skill-premium work also carries co-originators who are not credited, and it is not clear a three-name set can describe it fairly. An Autor-Dorn-Hanson citation avoids both problems. It credits the evidence and the designs, it does not claim origination of the task framework (Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu remain outside it), and it does not restate the 2023 or 2024 citations. On the chair's questions: (1) I would not support a two-name Autor-Hanson prize, because it would drop a lead author of the China-shock papers when the cap does not require it. (2) The committee does not need to resolve the shift-share and persistence debate. The established finding is that import exposure measurably reduced local employment and earnings, and that adjustment was slow and uneven. The magnitude of the long-run effect is contested, and the citation should say nothing on it. (3) The 2023 and 2024 prizes covered the history of women's labour-market outcomes and institutions and prosperity. They did not recognise the local-labour-market evidence on trade exposure, so I treat the adjacency as a framing and timing matter and not as prior recognition. I record that ten of eleven round-1 files name B006. I do not count that as merit, and my change of name runs against the majority set. My assessment also does not depend on the other files. I would reach the same view of the credit problem if I had not seen them.
statement.case_against: My configuration is still open to attack. Dorn's contribution to the task and polarisation strand is smaller than Autor's. Dropping Katz removes the long-run skill-premium framework, which supplies the interpretive structure behind the trade evidence, and several colleagues rate that strand as distinct and mature. The citation may still read as a composite of technology and trade. The shift-share inference concerns and the persistence and external-validity debate are unresolved, and the evidence is mostly from the US experience. Levy and Murnane remain a genuine omission. The Dorn-for-Katz swap is a judgement about credit and framing and not a finding that Katz's work is weaker. If colleagues judge that the breadth of the skill-premium strand outweighs the single-discovery framing, Autor, Hanson and Katz is a defensible set and I would not call it an error. If the committee views B006 as irreparably two discoveries, my cleaner alternatives are B012, which has clearer credit but a shorter record, and B001, which has broad influence but contested legal-origins identification.

responses.point: Andersson answers my round-1 question on coherence by saying one citation can hold both strands, since both concern how exposure to technology and trade shifts labour demand and distributes adjustment costs. He keeps Katz and says Dorn's contribution sits within a strand where Autor and Hanson already carry the design.
responses.response: I agree that one citation can hold both strands, and I have worded mine that way. I do not agree that Dorn is redundant. My round-1 file did not rely on seniority. I am arguing that Dorn is a lead co-author on the China-shock designs and also co-authored the polarisation work with Autor. That makes him a bridge between the two strands, and I think it is a better reason for the third name than the weight of the skill-premium strand. It is my reading of the record and not something I have verified independently. I accept Andersson's point that the citation should centre on labour-demand adjustment, and I have kept the wording to that. My change from Katz to Dorn is a judgement about credit, and I regard Andersson's version as a reasonable alternative.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson asks whether the committee would prefer Dorn over Katz for the trade-shock design. She keeps Katz for his skill-premium and wage-structure framework, but says Dorn for Katz is a defensible swap and she would not object strongly if the committee drew the line there.
responses.response: This is the question I now answer with Dorn. I accept her point that Katz's wage-structure work is distinct and widely used, and that it is not just the education-race book. My difficulty is that the skill-premium framework has co-originators who are not credited, and the part that is most associated with Katz overlaps with the Goldin recognition. A trade-and-technology citation anchored in the design-based evidence is easier to defend with clear credit. I also take her point that the framework gives the evidence its explanatory frame. The citation has to say what has been shown, and I think the evidence is the narrower and safer claim. Her stated flexibility suggests this may not be a hard disagreement between us.

responses.point: Enflo says Katz's best-known education-technology work was with a recent laureate, so his marginal credit overlaps with an earlier prize. She calls Katz the most contestable name in her configuration and says she wants the committee's view on the Katz-Goldin overlap before settling.
responses.response: I give my view on that overlap here. I agree with her reading and treat it as a real weakness, not just a matter of wording. I had earlier said Katz's claim was the most exposed part of my trio, and having reconsidered it I now think the exposure is large enough to change the name. I disagree with her only on remedy: she would handle the overlap through the citation wording, and I think a citation that avoids the overlap by naming different people is more robust. Her point that the local-labour-market evidence is the least duplicated part of B006 is one I share, and it is the reason my citation is built on that evidence.

responses.point: Friberg proposes only Autor and Hanson for B006, ranks it sixth and prefers B007. He reads B006 as two related lines, and says a three-name set spans both but leaves Dorn out and places Katz's work with Goldin next to a 2023 prize.
responses.response: I agree with his diagnosis of the Katz-Goldin problem and I have partly acted on it. I do not follow him to two names. The cap allows three, and dropping Dorn, a lead author of the China-shock papers, would make the award weaker on credit without any gain in clarity. I read the evidence as one body of work on how technology and trade exposure shift labour demand, and I name the person who links the lines. I also take his point that the credit division should be settled before B006 is treated as one clean discovery. I think my citation does that. On his preference for B007, I agree its attribution is cleaner. My reservation is the weaker identification of the constitutional and electoral-rule effects, and the fact that this reservation sits on the empirical side is why I keep B007 fifth.

responses.point: Krusell now ranks B006 first. He prefers Katz to Dorn, because Katz anchors the long-run framework linking technology, education and wage structure, and says dropping Katz would narrow the citation to the trade-shock evidence. He keeps B007 as an alternative and discloses that Persson is at his home institute.
responses.response: I agree that dropping Katz narrows the citation, and I do not hide that cost. My difference with him is how much the long-run framework needs a credited name when it has uncredited co-originators and overlaps with the 2023 prize. He treats Dorn's exclusion as a cost of the cap, and I treat Katz's exclusion as the lesser cost. Both are judgements and I do not claim his is wrong. On B007, I note the disclosure without adjudicating it, and I note that his ranking of B006 first does not depend on it. My own reservation about B007 is the identification of the cross-country results and not the credit.

responses.point: Boppart treats the Dorn-versus-Katz choice as the most important open question on B006. He says Dorn's claim on the China-shock papers is closer than Katz's and that Autor, Dorn and Hanson is a defensible substitution if the committee prefers a trade-shock-centred citation. He keeps Katz for breadth across technology and trade.
responses.response: I take his substitution as the starting point for my configuration, and I agree that Dorn's claim on the China-shock papers is closer than Katz's. Where I would add a point is that Dorn's work with Autor on polarisation also touches the technology strand. That means the substituted citation is not only about trade. I do not see this as settled. His preference for breadth is a coherent view, and I put the weight on the single-discovery framing and the clearer credit. I agree with him that Levy and Murnane are a genuine omission that the cap forces, and the citation should not claim the task lineage.

uncertainties: Whether Dorn or Katz is the better third name. I have moved to Dorn on credit and overlap grounds, but I regard this as a judgement call and not a settled one.
Whether the committee reads technology and trade as one body of work or as two. My claim that Dorn links the strands is my own reading of the credited names and is not independently verified.

How far the shift-share inference concerns, the persistence of China-shock effects and their external validity beyond the US should weigh on the citation. I would keep the wording to what has been shown on labour demand and local adjustment.
Whether the 2023 and 2024 prizes reduce the marginal case for B006, which depends on how narrowly the citation can be framed.
Whether the headline count of ten of eleven for B006 rests on the criteria or on convergence after reading openings. I cannot tell from the files alone.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson or Katz is apparent from my supplied profile. None of them appears among my listed co-authors or institutional affiliations. I disclose my adjunct appointment at Chicago Booth for transparency only. B001 (law and finance) and B012 (household debt and credit) are adjacent to my corporate-finance field, and B001 and B012 are my listed alternatives. I apply the same criteria as for every other field and do not adjudicate this. My earlier service on and chairing of the committee is background and not evidence of a prize preference. I note the round-1 disclosures from colleagues (Krusell on Persson, Boppart, Hassler and others) without adjudicating them.
